Working with Binomial and Normal distributions

Binomial distribution

Suppose we randomly sample 10 people, and define Y = number of people in sample who are left-handed. The probability of a random person being left-handed is 0.15.

What is the probability that exactly one person in the sample is left-handed?

R has a built in function for evaluating binomial probabilities:

dbinom(x=1, size=10, prob=0.15)
## [1] 0.3474254

What is the probability that at most 2 people are left-handed?

(That means either 0, 1, or 2 people in the sample are left-handed)

dbinom(x=0, size=10, prob=0.15) + dbinom(x=1, size=10, prob=0.15) + dbinom(x=2, size=10, prob=0.15)
## [1] 0.8201965

We can add up the individual probabilities (above), or we could use the cumulative distribution function:

pbinom(q=2, size=10, prob=0.15)
## [1] 0.8201965

We might also be interested in the 95th percentile of the distribution. In other words, what is the smallest number k such that the probability of having at most k left-handed people is at least 0.95?

We know from the previous example that 2 isn’t enough to get us to 95% cumulative probability. Is 3 enough?

pbinom(q=2, size=10, prob=0.15) #probability of at most 2 left handed
## [1] 0.8201965
pbinom(q=3, size=10, prob=0.15) #probability of at most 3 left handed
## [1] 0.9500302

Yes, the probability of having at most 3 left-handed people in a sample of 10 is >= 0.95.

Another way to get the 95th percentile is to use the built-in quantile function:

qbinom(p=0.95, size=10, prob=0.15)
## [1] 3

sampling from the binomial distribution

R also has built-in functions for drawing random samples from a binomial distribution.

Imagine flipping a fair coin 5 times. The sum of the 5 flips is Binomial(n=5, p=0.5).

We can simulate flipping a fair coin 5 times:

sample(c("heads", "tails"), size=5, replace=TRUE, prob=c(0.5,0.5))
## [1] "tails" "heads" "tails" "tails" "tails"

Replace “heads” and “tails” with 1 and 0:

sample(c(0,1), size=5, replace=TRUE, prob=c(0.5, 0.5))
## [1] 1 1 1 0 0

Take the sum to count the number of “heads” in the 5 flips:

sum(sample(c(0,1), size=5, replace=TRUE, prob=c(0.5, 0.5)))
## [1] 0

The sum of the 5 flips is Binomial(n=5, p=0.5).

R has a built in function for sampling from a binomial distribution

Draw one sample from Binom(n=5,p=0.5)- i.e., flip a coin 5 times and count the number of heads

rbinom(n=1, size=5, prob=0.5) # "size" and "prob" are the parameters of the binomial distribution
## [1] 3
                      #"n" is the number of samples we want to draw from the binomial distribution

Imagine we repeat the 5-coin-flip experiment 10 times, and record the number of heads each time.

From the probability distribution, E(# heads) = 2.5

y_values<- rbinom(n=10, size=5, prob=0.5) 
print(y_values)
##  [1] 2 2 2 4 2 2 1 3 1 1

What are the sample mean and variance for these 10 observations?

mean(y_values)
## [1] 2
sd(y_values)^2 #sample variance = sample standard deviation ^2
## [1] 0.8888889

We could repeat this entire exercise and get 10 new samples from the Binomial (10, 0.5) distribution:

y_values<-rbinom(n=10, size=5, prob=0.5)
mean(y_values)
## [1] 2.1
sd(y_values)^2
## [1] 0.7666667

The expected value and variance of the probability distribution don’t change.

But the properties of the sample data are different each time we draw a new random sample.

We can also visually compare the sampled data to the underlying binomial distribution.

We can make a bar graph of the true probability distribution. First, calculate the probability of each possible number of heads in 5 flips:

y_probs<-dbinom(x=0:5, size=5, prob=0.5) # "x" is the value for which you want to evaluate the probability, i.e. P(X=x)

#the notation x=0:5 evaluates the function at each value from 0 to 5

Then create a bar graph of those values:

barplot(y_probs, names.arg=0:5, xlab="y", ylab="P(Y=y)")

Make a frequency histogram of the sample data:

hist(y_values, xlab="y", breaks=0:5)

Note- the “breaks” argument controls how many buckets your range of values gets split into. If you don’t include that argument, R usually does a good job of choosing this automatically.

Histograms can have frequency on the Y axis, or relative frequency, i.e. the proportion of times that outcome came up.

hist(y_values, xlab="y", breaks=0:5, probability=TRUE)

Normal distribution

Suppose the population distribution of systolic blood pressure is Normal(120, 15^2)

What does the probability distribution function look like?

curve(dnorm(x, mean=120, sd=15), from=70, to=170, ylab="p(x)")

What is the probability that a randomly chosen person has blood pressure less than 115?

pnorm(q=115, mean=120, sd=15)
## [1] 0.3694413

By default, the “pnorm” function gives us the area under the curve, to the LEFT of the specified value.

What if we want the area under the curve, to the RIGHT of the specified value?

What is the probability that a randomly chosen person has blood pressure higher than 115?

1-pnorm(q=115, mean=120, sd=15)
## [1] 0.6305587

What is the probability that a randomly chosen person has blood pressure between 120 and 130? P(120 < X < 130) = P(X < 130) - P(X < 120)

xvals<-seq(from=70, to=130, by=0.01)
yvals<-dnorm(xvals, mean=120, sd=15)

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
curve(dnorm(x, mean=120, sd=15), from=70, to=170, ylab="p(x)")
polygon(c(min(xvals), xvals[xvals<=130], 130), c(0,yvals[xvals<=130], 0), col="cornflowerblue")

curve(dnorm(x, mean=120, sd=15), from=70, to=170, ylab="p(x)")
polygon(c(min(xvals), xvals[xvals<=130], 130), c(0,yvals[xvals<=130], 0), col="cornflowerblue")
polygon(c(min(xvals), xvals[xvals<=120], 120), c(0,yvals[xvals<=120], 0), col="orange")

First we find the blue shaded area, then subtract off the orange shaded area:

pnorm(q=130, mean=120, sd=15) - pnorm(q=120, mean=120, sd=15)
## [1] 0.2475075

What is the 95th quantile of the blood pressure distribution? I.e. what is the smallest value b such that P(X<b) >= 0.95?

In the binomial example about left-handedness, we could manually check each value to figure this out. Here, blood pressure is continuous, so it’s not feasible to find the value that way.

pnorm(q=130, mean=120, sd=15)
## [1] 0.7475075
pnorm(q=140, mean=120, sd=15)
## [1] 0.9087888
pnorm(q=145, mean=120, sd=15)
## [1] 0.9522096

Instead we use the built-in quantile function:

qnorm(p=0.95, mean=120, sd=15)
## [1] 144.6728

Now let’s draw samples from the normal distribution.

Sample 10 people’s blood pressure:

bp_samples<- rnorm(n=10, mean=120, sd=15)
bp_samples
##  [1] 138.5260 130.3874 141.2093 113.7057 117.9678 112.3427 133.9412 119.2038
##  [9] 123.0592 127.3736

What are the sample average and standard deviation?

mean(bp_samples)
## [1] 125.7717
sd(bp_samples)
## [1] 10.15943

We can visualize the sample data with a histogram:

hist(bp_samples, probability=TRUE, breaks=10, xlab="blood pressure (systolic)")

With only 10 samples, it’s quite chunky, and doesn’t look much like the bell curve of the underlying probability distribution.

What if we sample 100 people instead of 10?

set.seed(3218) 

bp_samples<-rnorm(n=100, mean=120, sd=15)
hist(bp_samples, breaks=15, probability=TRUE, xlab="blood pressure (systolic)")

The histogram of 100 sampled data points is starting to look a bit more like the shape of the normal distribution.

We can superimpose the probability distribution function on the histogram of sample values:

hist(bp_samples, breaks=15, probability=TRUE, xlab="blood pressure (systolic)")
curve(dnorm(x, mean=120, sd=15), from=70, to=170, add=TRUE)
